sounds.label: i as in lit
sounds.how: Spread your lips as if smiling and push the tongue high and forward. It is like the 'ee' in 'see', but shorter and tenser, with no 'y' glide at the end.
sounds.sentence: Il lit dans son lit à midi.

sounds.label: é as in été
sounds.how: Lips spread, tongue high and forward, mouth almost closed. Like the 'ay' in 'say', but cut off before the 'y' glide. Keep the muscles tense and steady from start to finish.
sounds.sentence: J'ai mangé au café cet été.

sounds.label: è as in mère
sounds.how: Drop the jaw a little more than for é and relax the lips. Close to the 'e' in 'bed'. Spellings: è, ê, ai, and e before two consonants (elle, merci).
sounds.sentence: Ma mère fait la fête.

sounds.label: a as in chat
sounds.how: Open the mouth wide with the tongue low and slightly forward. Somewhere between the 'a' in 'cat' and the 'a' in 'father'. Never reduce it to the 'uh' of English 'sofa'.
sounds.sentence: Le chat de mon ami est là.

sounds.label: â as in pâte
sounds.how: Open the mouth wide and pull the tongue back, as for the 'a' in 'father' or British 'car'. In Quebec this back â is very clearly different from the front a and often slightly rounded, toward 'aw'.
sounds.sentence: Le gâteau du château est en pâte.

sounds.label: o as in beau
sounds.how: Round the lips into a small tight circle and keep them still. Like the 'o' in 'go', but without the 'w' glide at the end. Spellings: eau, au, ô, and o at the end of a word.
sounds.sentence: Il fait beau au bord de l'eau.

sounds.label: o as in porte
sounds.how: Open the jaw more and round the lips loosely. Close to the vowel in British 'lot' or the start of 'thought'. Usually o followed by a pronounced consonant (porte, bol, homme).
sounds.sentence: L'homme ouvre la porte de l'école.

sounds.label: ou as in vous
sounds.how: Pull the tongue back and push tightly rounded lips forward, like the 'oo' in 'food' but tenser, with no glide. Spelled ou.
sounds.sentence: Nous jouons tous les jours.

sounds.label: u as in tu
sounds.how: No English equivalent. Say 'ee' as in 'see' and freeze your tongue there, then round and push your lips forward as if to whistle or say 'oo'. Tongue of 'ee' plus lips of 'oo'.
sounds.sentence: Tu as vu la rue?

sounds.label: eu as in deux
sounds.how: Put your tongue in position for é (as in 'say'), then round your lips as for 'o'. The mouth is almost closed. Usually eu at the end of a word or before a z sound (deux, heureuse).
sounds.sentence: Il veut deux jeux bleus.

sounds.label: eu as in fleur
sounds.how: Put your tongue in position for è (as in 'bed'), then round your lips loosely. A bit like the vowel in British 'fur' (no r), but with rounded lips. Usually eu or œu before a pronounced consonant.
sounds.sentence: Ma sœur a peur des fleurs.

sounds.label: e muet as in le
sounds.how: A short relaxed vowel with slightly rounded lips, like the 'a' in 'about' but rounded. It appears in small words (le, de, je, que) and in unstressed syllables (petit, demain).
sounds.sentence: Je te le redemande demain.

sounds.label: dropping the e muet
sounds.how: In normal speech the e muet often disappears when only one consonant comes before it: samedi sounds like 'sam-di', petit like 'p-ti', je ne sais pas like 'je n'sais pas'. Keep it when dropping it would pile up three consonants (vendredi, quelque chose). Quebec speakers drop it even more often.
sounds.sentence: Samedi, je ne sais pas ce que je fais.

sounds.label: an/en as in enfant
sounds.how: Open the mouth as for a, then let air flow through your nose as well as your mouth. Do NOT pronounce an n or ng at the end; the nose does the work. Spellings: an, am, en, em.
sounds.sentence: Les enfants chantent dans le vent.

sounds.label: on as in bon
sounds.how: Round the lips tightly as for the o in 'go' and send air through the nose. A bit like the 'on' of 'song' with the ng sound removed. Spellings: on, om.
sounds.sentence: Mon oncle a un bon nom.

sounds.label: in/ain/ein as in vin
sounds.how: Spread the lips as for è in 'bed' and send air through the nose. Similar to the vowel in 'bang' with no ng. Spellings: in, im, ain, aim, ein, and en after i (bien).
sounds.sentence: Le matin, j'ai faim de pain.

sounds.label: un as in brun
sounds.how: The rounded version of 'in': start with 'in' and round your lips. Many Paris speakers merge it with 'in', but in Quebec it stays clearly distinct, so it is worth learning.
sounds.sentence: Lundi, un ami brun porte du parfum.

sounds.label: nasal vowel vs pronounced n
sounds.how: When n or m is followed by a vowel (often a final e), the vowel stops being nasal and you pronounce a real n: bon vs bonne, fin vs fine. This is how many masculine and feminine forms differ.
sounds.sentence: Un bon vin et une bonne bière.

sounds.label: y glide as in pied
sounds.how: Like the 'y' in 'yes', said quickly and attached to the next vowel. Spellings: i or y before a vowel (pied, payer), ill, final il (travail).
sounds.sentence: Viens bien t'asseoir à mes pieds.

sounds.label: w glide as in oui
sounds.how: Like the 'w' in 'we': start with ou and slide quickly into the next vowel. Spellings: ou before a vowel (oui, jouer), and the w part of oi.
sounds.sentence: Oui, Louis va jouer à l'ouest.

sounds.label: ui as in huit
sounds.how: Start with the French u of 'tu' (tongue forward, lips rounded) and slide fast into i. It is NOT 'wee': keep the tongue forward. Compare lui and Louis.
sounds.sentence: Depuis minuit, il cuisine pour lui.

sounds.label: oi as in moi
sounds.how: The spelling oi is always said 'wa', like 'wa' in 'wander'. In casual Quebec speech you will also hear 'moé' and 'toé' for moi and toi (see the Quebec section).
sounds.sentence: Ce soir, je vais boire un verre avec toi.

sounds.label: French r as in rouge
sounds.how: Keep the tip of your tongue down behind your lower teeth. Raise the back of the tongue toward the soft back of the roof of your mouth and let air rub there, like a soft gargle or a voiced version of the 'ch' in Scottish 'loch'. Never curl the tongue like English r.
sounds.sentence: Robert rentre à trois heures.

sounds.label: u vs ou
sounds.how: The most important vowel contrast for English speakers. For u, the tongue stays forward ('ee' position) with rounded lips. For ou, the tongue pulls back ('oo' in 'food'). Feel your tongue slide back as you go from tu to tout.
sounds.sentence: Le chat est dessus, pas dessous.

sounds.label: é vs è
sounds.how: é is closed and tense, lips spread ('say' without the y). è is open and relaxed ('bed'). Spelling clues: é, -er, -ez are closed; è, ê, -ait, -ais and e before two consonants are open. Quebec keeps parlé and parlait clearly different.
sounds.sentence: J'ai parlé à Marie pendant qu'elle parlait au téléphone.

sounds.label: liaison
sounds.how: A normally silent final consonant is pronounced and joined to the next word when that word starts with a vowel sound. s and x become z (les amis = 'lé-za-mi'), d becomes t (grand homme), n links (un ami). Required after determiners and pronouns (les, des, mon, nous, vous). Never after 'et' and never before h aspiré.
sounds.sentence: Nous avons deux amis aux États-Unis.

sounds.label: enchaînement
sounds.how: A consonant that is always pronounced slides onto the next word's first vowel, so the words flow together in one breath: 'il a' sounds like 'i-la', 'une amie' like 'u-na-mie'. French speech is a stream of syllables, not separate words.
sounds.sentence: Elle habite avec une amie à Ottawa.

sounds.label: h muet
sounds.how: French h is never pronounced. With most h-words (h muet), the word behaves as if it starts with a vowel: elision (l'homme) and liaison (les hommes = 'lé-zom') happen as normal.
sounds.sentence: Les hommes arrivent à l'hôpital.

sounds.label: h aspiré
sounds.how: The h is still silent, but it acts like a wall: no elision (le héros, not l'héros) and no liaison (les haricots without a z). Learn these words by heart: héros, haricot, honte, haut, hockey, hibou, huit.
sounds.sentence: Les héros du hockey sont en haut.

sounds.label: gn as in montagne
sounds.how: Press the middle of your tongue flat against the roof of your mouth, like the 'ny' in 'canyon' or the 'ni' in 'onion', as one sound.
sounds.sentence: À la campagne, l'agneau regarde la montagne.

sounds.label: ill as in fille
sounds.how: After a vowel or in most words, ill is the 'y' sound of 'yes': fille = 'fiy', travailler = 'tra-va-yé', soleil = 'so-ley'. A few common exceptions keep a real l: ville, mille, tranquille.
sounds.sentence: La fille de la famille travaille au soleil.

sounds.label: silent final consonants
sounds.how: Most final consonants are silent: s, t, d, x, z, p (petit, grand, deux). A handy rule is CaReFuL: final c, r, f, l are usually pronounced (sac, mer, chef, sel), except -er in verbs and many nouns (parler, premier). A final e makes the consonant before it pronounced (petite, grande).
sounds.sentence: Le petit chef a un grand sac de sel.

sounds.label: silent -ent in verbs
sounds.how: The -ent ending of ils/elles verbs is completely silent: ils parlent sounds exactly like il parle. Careful: in nouns and adverbs like moment or souvent, -ent is the nasal 'an'.
sounds.sentence: Ils parlent souvent et ils mangent lentement.

sounds.label: s vs z
sounds.how: A single s between two vowels is a z sound (poison, rose). Double ss is always s (poisson). Mixing them up changes the word: poisson is fish, poison is poison.
sounds.sentence: Mon cousin mange du poisson au dessert.

sounds.label: ch and j
sounds.how: ch is the 'sh' of 'shoe' (never the 'ch' of 'church'). j, and g before e or i, is the 's' of 'measure' (never the 'j' of 'jump'). Push the lips slightly forward for both.
sounds.sentence: Je cherche mon chat chaque jour.

sounds.label: p, t, k without a puff of air
sounds.how: English p, t, k at the start of a word come with a puff of air (hold a hand in front of your mouth and say 'pie'). French p, t, k have no puff. Also, French t and d touch the back of the upper teeth, not the gum ridge.
sounds.sentence: Papa a pris un café à Paris.

quebec.label: t and d before i/u
quebec.how: Before i, u (and the glides of 'lui', 'tiens'), t becomes 'ts' and d becomes 'dz'. This is standard Quebec pronunciation used by everyone in every register, including the news. Not slang.
examples: Ma tante habite dans une petite ville.

quebec.label: short i, u, ou in closed syllables
quebec.how: When i, u or ou are in the last syllable and followed by a pronounced consonant (except r, z, v, j sounds), they become short and relaxed: vite sounds like English 'vit' (as in 'bit'), poule like English 'pull'. Standard in Quebec, all registers.

quebec.label: gliding long vowels
quebec.how: Long vowels in a stressed final syllable often glide into a second vowel: père sounds like 'paère', fête like 'faète', pâte like 'pâoute', fleur like 'flaeur'. Mild gliding is normal everywhere in Quebec; strong gliding is more casual or regional.
examples: Elle a mis la pâte au four.

quebec.label: â vs a (and final a)
quebec.how: Quebec keeps a clear difference between front a (patte) and back â (pâte), which sounds close to 'aw'. In casual speech, an a at the very end of a word is also pulled back: Canada, chat, ça sound like 'Canadâ', 'châ', 'çâ'. The final-a version is informal.
examples: Le chat a mal à la patte.
On mange des pâtes au Canada.

quebec.label: ê kept distinct from è
quebec.how: Quebec keeps a long ê (often gliding) separate from a short è, a contrast many Paris speakers have lost: mettre vs maître, faites vs fête. The long one sounds like 'aè'.

quebec.label: -er / -ère / -erre sounding like 'aère'
quebec.how: Before r, è opens toward a and often glides: père, mère, frère, hiver, terre sound like 'paère', 'maère', 'fraère', 'hivaère'. A slight opening is common in all speech. The strong 'a' version (merci said 'marci', perdre said 'pardre') is informal and somewhat stereotyped.
examples: Ma mère est sur la terrasse.

quebec.label: moé / toé (informal)
quebec.how: In casual, older or rural speech, moi and toi are said 'moé' and 'toé'. Very common in songs, sitcoms and family talk; younger urban speakers mostly say moi/toi. Understand it, but use moi/toi yourself unless you are sure of the setting. INFORMAL.

quebec.label: oi said 'è' in some words (informal)
quebec.how: In a handful of very common words, oi becomes an è sound: droit becomes 'drette' (drette là = right there), froid becomes 'frette' (il fait frette = it's freezing), étroit becomes 'étrette'. Fixed words only, not a general rule. INFORMAL.

quebec.label: final t pronounced in some words (informal)
quebec.how: Some words keep a final t that is silent in standard French: bout, debout, nuit, lit, and the feminine-looking 'toute' used for tout ('toutte'). Ici becomes 'icitte'. Very common in casual speech. INFORMAL.
examples: C'est au bout de la rue.

quebec.label: chu, t'sais, y'é, a (informal)
quebec.how: Subject pronouns and verbs fuse in fast speech: je suis becomes 'chu', tu sais becomes 't'sais' or 'tsé', il est becomes 'y'é', il y a becomes 'y'a', elle becomes 'a' ('a l'a dit'), ils becomes 'y'. Everyone uses these in casual talk; avoid them in writing and formal situations. INFORMAL.
quebec.std: je suis, tu sais, il est, elle a
examples: Tu sais, il est déjà parti.

quebec.label: su'a, dans'a (informal)
quebec.how: The l of la, le, les drops after short prepositions: sur la becomes 'su'a', sur le becomes 'su'l', dans la becomes 'dans'a', dans les becomes 'dans'é', à la becomes 'à'a'. Extremely frequent in conversation. INFORMAL.
quebec.std: sur la table, dans la cuisine, sur le bord
quebec.qc: su'a table, dans'a cuisine, su'l bord (informal)
examples: Le livre est sur la table.

quebec.label: the question particle -tu (informal)
quebec.how: Yes/no questions are often marked with 'tu' after the verb, whatever the subject: 'Tu veux-tu?', 'C'est-tu loin?', 'Ça marche-tu?'. With affrication it sounds like 'tsu'. Not the pronoun tu here, just a question marker. INFORMAL.
quebec.std: Tu veux du café? C'est loin?
quebec.qc: Tu veux-tu du café? C'est-tu loin? (informal)

quebec.label: Quebec nasal vowels
quebec.how: Quebec nasals sound different from Paris: 'an' is pronounced further forward (to French ears close to Paris 'in'), 'in' is tighter and may glide slightly, 'on' is tightly rounded, and 'un' stays distinct from 'in'. Standard Quebec, all registers.
quebec.qc: maman with a front nasal a (sounds like 'mamain' to Paris ears), vin tighter, un kept distinct from in
examples: Un bon vin blanc, s'il vous plaît.

quebec.label: whispered i and u
quebec.how: Between two voiceless consonants (p, t, k, f, s, ch), i and u are often whispered or almost disappear: piscine sounds like 'p'scine', épicerie like 'ép'cerie', politique like 'pol'tique'. Standard Quebec, very common.

quebec.label: rhythm, intonation and là
quebec.how: Like all French, stress falls on the last syllable of each word group, and syllables are fairly even. Quebec speech lengthens and glides stressed vowels, so it can sound more 'sing-song' or drawn out. The tag 'là' at the end of phrases is a filler or emphasis word ('Je m'en vais, là'). 'Bon ben' and 'pis' (for puis) are frequent fillers. Fillers are informal.
quebec.std: Je vais au dépanneur. Bon, eh bien, j'y vais. Et puis?
quebec.qc: Je vais au dépanneur, là. Bon ben, j'y vais. Pis? (informal)

quebec.label: the Quebec r
quebec.how: Today most Quebecers use the back-of-the-throat r, like in France. A rolled tongue-tip r was traditional in Montreal and western Quebec and is still heard from some older speakers. After a long vowel at the end of a word the r can be very weak.
quebec.qc: back r for most speakers; rolled tip r for some older Montrealers

twisters.fr: Les chaussettes de l'archiduchesse sont-elles sèches, archi-sèches?
twisters.en: Are the archduchess's socks dry, extra-dry?

twisters.fr: Un chasseur sachant chasser doit savoir chasser sans son chien.
twisters.en: A hunter who knows how to hunt must be able to hunt without his dog.

twisters.fr: Si six scies scient six cyprès, six cent six scies scient six cent six cyprès.
twisters.en: If six saws saw six cypresses, six hundred and six saws saw six hundred and six cypresses.

twisters.fr: Ton thé t'a-t-il ôté ta toux?
twisters.en: Did your tea get rid of your cough?
twisters.focus: t without a puff of air

twisters.fr: Didon dîna, dit-on, du dos d'un dodu dindon.
twisters.en: Dido dined, they say, on the back of a plump turkey.
twisters.focus: d, and on vs in nasals

twisters.fr: Je veux et j'exige d'exquises excuses.
twisters.en: I want and demand exquisite apologies.

twisters.fr: Trois tortues trottaient sur un trottoir très étroit.
twisters.en: Three turtles trotted on a very narrow sidewalk.

twisters.fr: Seize chaises sèchent.
twisters.en: Sixteen chairs are drying.

twisters.fr: Cinq chiens chassent six chats.
twisters.en: Five dogs chase six cats.

twisters.fr: Pauvre petit pêcheur, prends patience pour pouvoir prendre plusieurs petits poissons.
twisters.en: Poor little fisherman, be patient so you can catch several little fish.
twisters.focus: p without a puff of air

twisters.fr: Le ver vert va vers le verre vert.
twisters.en: The green worm goes toward the green glass.

twisters.fr: Natacha n'attacha pas son chat Pacha qui s'échappa.
twisters.en: Natacha didn't tie up her cat Pacha, who escaped.

twisters.fr: Dans ta tente, ta tante t'attend.
twisters.en: In your tent, your aunt is waiting for you.

twisters.fr: Suis-je bien chez ce cher Serge?
twisters.en: Am I really at dear Serge's place?

twisters.fr: Cent sans-cœur sans sang.
twisters.en: A hundred heartless people without blood.

twisters.fr: Il était une fois un homme de foi qui vendait du foie dans la ville de Foix.
twisters.en: Once upon a time there was a man of faith who sold liver in the town of Foix.

twisters.fr: Douze douches douces.
twisters.en: Twelve gentle showers.

twisters.fr: Pruneau cuit, pruneau cru.
twisters.en: Cooked prune, raw prune.

twisters.fr: Un pâtissier qui pâtissait chez un tapissier qui tapissait.
twisters.en: A pastry chef who baked at the home of an upholsterer who upholstered.

twisters.fr: Tu t'entêtes à tout tenter, tu t'uses et tu te tues à tant t'entêter.
twisters.en: You insist on trying everything; you wear yourself out and kill yourself by being so stubborn.
twisters.focus: u vs ou, t (affricated as ts in Quebec)
